knowledge_point.title: Finding an Area by Transforming to a Type I Region

question.:question/problem:
Using the change of variables 

$$
u=x - 2 y,\,v=y,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ bounded by the curve $(x - 2 y)^{2}-(y)=0$ and the line $y=36.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=x - 2 y,\,v=y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$

Substituting $x - 2 y=u$ and $y=v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
(x - 2 y)^{2}-(y)=0\,⟹\,u^{2}-v=0\,⟹\,v=u^{2}.
$$

while substituting $y=v$ into the equation of the second curve, we obtain

$$
v=36.
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}v=u^{2} \\ v=36\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,u=\pm 6\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm 6,36).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,-6\le u\le 6,\,u^{2}\le v\le 36\}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/generate/repairs/2026-10-20-early-cohort/jobs/17592186129197/workspace/evidence/runtime/plots/d207c4743dd010bb04819e34.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\left|\begin{matrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x}&\frac{∂u}{∂y}\\\frac{∂v}{∂x}&\frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{matrix}\right| \\ &=\left|\begin{matrix}1&-2\\0&1\end{matrix}\right| \\ &=1\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=(1)^{-1}=1.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D dxdy &=\iint_Δ |\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,dudv \\ &=\iint_Δ |1|\,dudv \\ &=1\int_{-6}^{6}[\int_{u^{2}}^{36}dv]du \\ &=1\int_{-6}^{6}[v]_{u^{2}}^{36}du \\ &=1\int_{-6}^{6}(36)-(u^{2})du \\ &=1\int_{-6}^{6}(36 - u^{2})du \\ &=1[- \frac{u^{3}}{3} + 36 u]_{-6}^{6} \\ &=1(((216)+(-72))-((-216)+(72))) \\ &=1(288) \\ &=288\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding an Area by Transforming to a Type I Region

question.:question/problem:
Using the change of variables 

$$
u=2 x + y,\,v=- 2 x + y,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ bounded by the lines $2 x + y=3,$ $- 2 x + y=3$ and the curve $- 4 x^{2} + y^{2}=12.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=2 x + y,\,v=- 2 x + y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$

Substituting $2 x + y=u$ into the equation of the first line, we get

$$
2 x + y=3\,⟹\,u=3.
$$

while substituting $- 2 x + y=v$ into the equation of the second line, we obtain

$$
- 2 x + y=3\,⟹\,v=3.
$$

Substituting $u=2 x + y$ and $v=- 2 x + y$ into the equation of curve, we get

$$
- 4 x^{2} + y^{2}=12\,⟹\,(2 x + y)(- 2 x + y)=12\,⟹\,uv=12.
$$

The intersection point of the two lines in the $uv$-plane is $(3,3).$

To find the intersection of the curve with the first line in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}uv=12 \\ u=3\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}u=3 \\ v=4\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the intersections of the curve with the second line in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}uv=12 \\ v=3\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}v=3 \\ u=4\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(3,3),$ $(3,4)$ and $(4,3).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,3\le u\le 4,\,3\le v\le \frac{12}{u}\}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/generate/repairs/2026-10-20-early-cohort/jobs/17592186129197/workspace/evidence/runtime/plots/d825c13659bba3bd849500c0.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\left|\begin{matrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x}&\frac{∂u}{∂y}\\\frac{∂v}{∂x}&\frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{matrix}\right| \\ &=\left|\begin{matrix}2&1\\-2&1\end{matrix}\right| \\ &=4\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=(4)^{-1}=\frac{1}{4}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D dxdy &=\iint_Δ |\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,dudv \\ &=\iint_Δ |\frac{1}{4}|\,dudv \\ &=\frac{1}{4}\int_{3}^{4}[\int_{3}^{\frac{12}{u}}dv]du \\ &=\frac{1}{4}\int_{3}^{4}[v]_{3}^{\frac{12}{u}}du \\ &=\frac{1}{4}\int_{3}^{4}(\frac{12}{u})-(3)du \\ &=\frac{1}{4}[- 3 u + 12 \ln{\left(u \right)}]_{3}^{4} \\ &=\frac{1}{4}(((12 \ln{\left(4 \right)})+(-12))-((12 \ln{\left(3 \right)})+(-9))) \\ &=\frac{1}{4}(-3 + \ln{\left(\frac{16777216}{531441} \right)}) \\ &=- \frac{3}{4} + \ln{\left(\frac{64}{27} \right)}\end{aligned}
$$
